Course Objectives

No. Objectives
The course aims:
1
To introduce advanced concepts of transaction management and recovery techniques.
2
To impart knowledge related to query processing and query optimizer phases of a database 
management system
3
To introduce concepts of advanced access control techniques like role based and discretionary 
methods 
4
To introduce advanced database models like distributed databases and emerging data models 
like temporal, mobile and spatial databases. 
5
To introduce the concepts of Big Data technologies and frameworks used to store, process and 
analyze large-scale datasets for strategic decision making.
Course Outcomes
The student will be able to:
1
Explain and analyze the concept of a transaction, and evaluate how ACID properties are 
preserved during concurrent transactions in a database
2
Measure and evaluate query costs, and design alternative efficient paths for optimized query 
execution
3 Apply and integrate advanced access control protocols to regulate and secure database usage
4
Create distributed database models and understand design of applications using advanced 
paradigms such as mobile and spatial databases

Transaction Concept 
Key Points:
• Consistency: Consistency means database remains in a valid state before and 
after a transaction. 
• Integrity: Integrity means the accuracy and correctness of data stored in the 
database. It ensures that all data follows defined rules and constraints such as 
primary key, foreign key, and domain constraints. 
• Reliability: Reliability means the ability of the database system to function 
correctly even in the presence of failures such as system crashes, power 
failures, or errors.

Transaction Property
❖To ensure integrity of data, the database system must ensure:
1. Atomicity
2. Consistency

1.Atomicity
• A transaction should be atomic, meaning it is executed completely or not at all. 
• A transaction cannot be executed partially. 
• Either all operations of the transaction are properly reflected in the database or none are.

• A valid state follows all rules, constraints, and relationships (primary key, 
foreign key, etc.). 
• Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves the consistency of the 
database.

3. Isolation
• Isolation ensures that transactions execute independently without interfering with

• Changes made by one transaction are not visible to others until they are committed. 
• It ensures that concurrent transactions give the same result as serial execution.

slides.text:
Durability
• Durability ensures that once a transaction is committed, its changes are permanently 
stored in the database, even if a system crash or failure occurs.
• After a transaction commits, the data is written to non-volatile storage (disk). 
• Even if the system crashes immediately after commit, the database can recover the 
committed data using logs or backups. 
• No committed data will be lost. 
Example:
After transferring money from Account A to Account B:
The updated balances are saved on disk. 
Even if the system crashes right after commit, the transaction remains intact after 
recovery.

slides.text:
ACID Properties- Example of Fund Transfer
• Transaction to transfer $50 from account A to account B: 
1. read(A) 
2. A := A – 50 
3. write(A) 
4. read(B) 
5. B := B + 50 
6. write(B)
• Consistency requirement – the sum of A and B is unchanged by the execution of the 
transaction.
• Atomicity requirement — if the transaction fails after step 3 and before step 6, the 
system should ensure that its updates are not reflected in the database, else an 
inconsistency will result.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 25

slides.text:
ACID Properties- Example of Fund Transfer
• Durability requirement — once the user has been notified that the transaction has 
completed (i.e., the transfer of the $50 has taken place), the updates to the database 
by the transaction must persist despite failures.
• Isolation requirement — if between steps 3 and 6, another transaction is allowed to 
access the partially updated database, it will see an inconsistent database (the sum A + 
B will be less than it should be).
• Can be ensured trivially by running transactions serially, that is one after the other. 
• However, executing multiple transactions concurrently has significant benefits, as we will see.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 26

slides.text:
Implementation of Atomicity and 
Durability
❖The recovery-management component of a database system implements the 
support for atomicity and durability.
❖The shadow-database scheme:
➢assume that only one transaction is active at a time.
➢a pointer called db_pointer always points to the current consistent copy of 
the database.
➢all updates are made on a shadow copy of the database, and db_pointer is 
made to point to the updated shadow copy only after the transaction 
reaches partial commit and all updated pages have been flushed to disk.
➢in case transaction fails, old consistent copy pointed to by db_pointer can 
be used, and the shadow copy can be deleted.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 27

Durability
The shadow-database scheme:
• Assumes disks to not fail.
• Useful for text editors, but extremely inefficient for large databases: executing 
a single transaction requires copying the entire database.

slides.text:
Concurrent Executions
❖ Multiple transactions are allowed to run concurrently in the system.
❖ Advantages are:
❖improved throughput and increased processor and disk utilization, leading 
to better transaction throughput: one transaction can be using the CPU 
while another is reading from or writing to the disk 
❖Reduced waiting time and reduced average response time for transactions: 
short transactions need not wait behind long ones.
❖ Concurrency control schemes – mechanisms to achieve isolation, i.e., to 
control the interaction among the concurrent transactions in order to prevent 
them from destroying the consistency of the database.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 29

Schedule
A schedule is an ordered sequence of operations (read, write, commit, etc.) from 
one or more transactions, representing how the transactions are executed in the 
database system.
Key Points
A schedule determines the execution order of operations from multiple 
transactions 
It can include: 
◦ Operations of a single transaction, or 
◦ Interleaved operations of multiple transactions 
It preserves the order of operations within each transaction

Serial Schedules in DBMS
❖A serial schedule is a schedule in which transactions are executed one after 
another, without any interleaving of operations.
❖Only one transaction executes at a time
❖The next transaction starts only after the previous one finishes

Recoverable

Cascadeless

Serial Schedules in DBMS
Problems with Serial Scheduling
Although serial schedules are safe and simple, they have several performance 
drawbacks:
1. More Waiting Time
2. Less Resource Utilization
3. Less Throughput
4. Late Response Time
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 34

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 35

Non-Serial Schedule 
A non-serial schedule is a schedule in which multiple transactions execute 
concurrently, and their operations are interleaved (mixed) with each other.
Key Characteristics
Non-serial schedules are NOT always: Consistent, Recoverable, Cascadeless.
Advantages
Reduced Waiting Time: Transactions do not wait for others to complete 
Increased Resource Utilization: CPU, memory, and I/O are used efficiently 
Decreased Response Time: Faster execution for individual transactions 
Higher Throughput: More transactions completed per unit time

Serializability
•Serializability is a concept in DBMS that ensures that even when transactions are 
executed concurrently (non-serially), the final result is equivalent to some serial 
(one-by-one) execution, thus maintaining a consistent database.
There are two ways to check whether any non-serial schedule is serializable.
1. Conflict Serializability
2. View Serializability

View Serializability
A schedule is said to be view serializable if it is view equivalent to some serial 
schedule.
View Equivalent Schedules
Two schedules (one serial and one non-serial) are said to be view equivalent if 
they satisfy the following conditions:
1. Initial Read: If a transaction reads the initial value of a data item in one 
schedule,
it must read the initial value in the other schedule also. 
2. Read-From Relationship: If a transaction reads a value written by another 
transaction, it must read from the same transaction in both schedules. 
3. Final Write: The last write operation on each data item must be done by the 
same transaction in both schedules.

Modes of lock:
1. Shared Lock (S) 
❖If a transaction Ti has obtained a shared-mode lock (denoted by S) on item Q, 
then Ti can read, but cannot write, Q.
❖ S-lock is requested using lock-S instruction.
2. Exclusive Lock (X) 
❖If a transaction Ti has obtained an exclusive-mode lock (denoted by X) on item 
Q, then Ti can both read and write Q.
❖X-lock is requested using lock-X instruction.

Lock-Based Protocols 
• We require that every transaction request a lock in an appropriate mode on data 
item Q, depending on the types of operations that it will perform on Q.
• The transaction makes the request to the concurrency-control manager.
• The transaction can proceed with the operation only after the concurrency￾control manager grants the lock to the transaction.
• The use of these two lock modes allows multiple transactions to read a data item 
but limits write access to just one transaction at a time.

• Two-phase locking does not ensure freedom from deadlocks.

• Rigorous two-phase locking: a transaction must hold all locks till commit/abort.

Timestamp-Based Protocols
•Timestamp-based protocols are concurrency control techniques that use timestamps instead 
of locks to ensure correct execution of transactions. Each transaction is assigned a unique 
timestamp when it starts, which determines its order.
•In the Timestamp Ordering Protocol, all operations must follow the chronological order of 
timestamps. If a transaction tries to read or write a data item in a way that violates this order, 
the transaction is rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp.
•This protocol maintains two timestamps for each data item: read timestamp (RTS) and write 
timestamp (WTS). These are used to decide whether an operation is allowed or should be 
rejected.
•The main advantage of timestamp-based protocols is that they are deadlock-free, since 
transactions do not wait for locks. However, they may lead to frequent rollbacks, which can 
reduce performance in high-contention systems.

• The timestamp ordering protocol ensures that any conflicting read and write 
operations are executed in timestamp order.

2. If TS(Ti)  W-timestamp(Q), then the read operation is executed, and R￾timestamp(Q) is set to max(R-timestamp(Q), TS(Ti)).

Necessary Conditions of Deadlock 
For a deadlock to occur in a DBMS, all four conditions must be true simultaneously:
1. Mutual Exclusion
Only one transaction can hold a resource (lock) at a time . Other transactions must wait if 
the resource is already locked 
2. Hold and Wait
A transaction is holding one resource .While waiting for another resource held by another 
transaction 
3. No Preemption
Resources (locks) cannot be forcibly taken away .They are released only by the transaction 
itself
4. Circular Wait
A cycle of transactions exists . Each transaction is waiting for a resource held by the next

slides.text:
Deadlock Handling
There are three main approaches to handle deadlocks. 
•The first is deadlock prevention, where the system ensures that deadlocks never occur by 
restricting how locks are requested. Techniques like wait-die and wound-wait use timestamps to 
decide which transaction should wait or be rolled back.
•The second approach is deadlock avoidance, where the system checks whether granting a lock 
request will lead to a deadlock. If there is a risk, the request is denied. This approach is less 
commonly used due to its complexity.
•The third approach is deadlock detection and recovery. In this method, the system allows 
deadlocks to occur but periodically checks for them using a wait-for graph. If a cycle is found, 
one transaction is selected as a victim and rolled back to break the deadlock.

• If TS(Ti) > TS(tj) − that is Ti is younger than Tj − then Ti dies. Ti is restarted later with a random 
delay but with the same timestamp. 
•This scheme allows the older transaction to wait but kills the younger one.

Wound-Wait Scheme
In this protocol, if a transaction requests to lock a resource (data item), which is already held 
with conflicting lock by some another transaction, one of the two possibilities may occur −
• If TS(Ti) < TS(Tj), then Ti forces Tj to be rolled back − that is Ti wounds Tj. Tj is restarted later 
with a random delay but with the same timestamp.
• If TS(Ti) > TS(Tj), then Ti is forced to wait until the resource is available. 
This protocol, allows the younger transaction to wait; but when an older transaction requests an 
item held by a younger one, the older transaction forces the younger one to abort and release 
the item.

Deadlock Detection
• Deadlocks can be described as a wait-for graph, which consists of a pair G = 
(V,E),
◦ V is a set of vertices (all the transactions in the system)
◦ E is a set of edges; each element is an ordered pair Ti →Tj
.
• If Ti → Tj is in E, then there is a directed edge from Ti to Tj, implying that Ti is 
waiting for Tj to release a data item.
• When Ti requests a data item currently being held by Tj, then the edge Ti → Tj is 
inserted in the wait-for graph. This edge is removed only when Tj is no longer 
holding a data item needed by Ti.

Deadlock Recovery
• When deadlock is detected:
• Some transaction will have to rolled back (made a victim) to break deadlock. Select 
that transaction as victim that will incur minimum cost.
• Rollback -- determine how far to roll back transaction.
• Total rollback: Abort the transaction and then restart it.
• More effective to roll back transaction only as far as necessary to break deadlock.
• Starvation happens if same transaction is always chosen as victim. Include the 
number of rollbacks in the cost factor to avoid starvation.

Recovery System: Recovery Concepts
• A computer system, like any other device, is subject to failure.
• Therefore, the database system must take actions in advance to ensure that the atomicity and 
durability properties of transactions are preserved.
• A recovery system ensures that the database remains consistent and correct even after failures 
like:
• System crash 
• Power failure 
• Transaction errors 
• The recovery scheme must also support high availability.

to ensure that failure during data transfer does not damage the needed information.

Shadow Paging
•Shadow Paging is alternative to log-based recovery.
•This scheme is useful if transactions execute serially. 
•It ensures ACID properties (atomicity and durability) without using logs
•It maintains two page tables.
1. Shadow Page Table (original, stable state) 
2. Current Page Table (for active updates). 
•Updates are made on a new copy, not on the original.
•It enables fast, instantaneous recovery by discarding the current table upon 
failure and switching tables upon commit.

Shadow Paging
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 18

Shadow Paging
Key Components and Working:
•Two Tables: When a transaction starts, the current page table is a copy of the 
shadow page table. Both point to the same pages on the disk.
•Out-of-Place Updates: When a page is modified, a new block is allocated on the 
disk, and the modification is written there. The current page table points to this 
new block, while the shadow page table still points to the old, unmodified block.
•Commit: To commit, the current page table becomes the new shadow page table, 
and the old disk blocks are freed.
•Abort/Recovery: If the transaction fails, the current page table is discarded, and 
the shadow table remains, effectively reversing changes without undo operations.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 19

Shadow Paging
Advantages:
Fast Recovery: No UNDO or REDO operations are required.
No Overhead: Eliminates the need for writing log records to the disk continuously. 
Disadvantages:
Data Fragmentation: Pages become scattered on the disk over time, reducing 
performance.
High Commit Cost: Committing requires updating the entire page table and clearing old 
pages, which is inefficient.
Concurrency Issues: Difficult to manage multiple concurrent transactions compared to 
log-based techniques

Checkpoints
• Redoing/undoing all transactions recorded in the log can be very slow
• Processing the entire log is time-consuming if the system has run for a long time
• We might unnecessarily redo transactions which have already output their updates to 
the database.
• Streamline recovery procedure by periodically performing checkpointing
•1. Output all log records currently residing in main memory onto stable storage.
•2. Output all modified buffer blocks to the disk.
•3. Write a log record < checkpoint L> onto stable storage where L is a list of all 
transactions active at the time of checkpoint.
•4. All updates are stopped while doing checkpointing

ARIES
• ARIES- Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics 
•ARIES is the most widely used database recovery algorithm in modern Database 
Management Systems (DBMS). 
• It was developed by IBM and is used in systems such as IBM Db2 and has influenced 
recovery mechanisms in many other database systems.
• Its purpose is to recover the database after a system crash while ensuring the ACID 
properties, especially Atomicity and Durability.
• It incorporates numerous optimizations to reduce overheads during normal processing and to 
speed up recovery.
• It is designed to improve concurrency, reduce logging overhead and reduce recovery time.

Physiological redo
• Affected page is physically identified, action within page can be logical
• Used to reduce logging overheads
• e.g. when a record is deleted and all other records have to be moved to fill hole
• Physiological redo can log just the record deletion
• Physical redo would require logging of old and new values for much of the page
• Requires page to be output to disk atomically
• Easy to achieve with hardware RAID, also supported by some disk systems
• Incomplete page output can be detected by checksum techniques
• But extra actions are required for recovery.

Operations on Files
System Control Operations
 These operations handle the setup, closing, and background optimization of 
files.
 Open: Allocates buffer memory and prepares the file for read or write 
modes.
 Close: Releases the allocated memory buffer, saves remaining changes, 
and revokes access to the file.
 Reset: Re-positions the active file pointer back to the very first record.
 Reorganize: Re-arranges the internal layout of records. This reclaims wasted 
storage space left behind by deleted entries and improves performance.

slides.text: Indexing

Indexing
Advantages of Indexing in DBMS
1.Faster Data Retrieval: Indices allow quick access to records without
scanning the entire table.
2.Improved Query Performance: Enhances the efficiency of SELECT queries,
JOINs, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY operations.
3.Support for Uniqueness: Enforces unique constraints on columns like primary
keys to maintain data integrity.
4.Reduced I/O Operations: Minimizes disk access by providing direct pointers
to data locations.
5.Efficient Sorting: Maintains data in sorted order, speeding up ORDER BY and
range queries.

Indexing
Disadvantages of Indexing in DBMS
1.Slower Write Operations: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE become slightly slower
because indices must be updated.
2.Additional Storage Required: Indices consume extra disk space depending
on their type and size.
3.Maintenance Overhead: Indices need periodic updates, which adds
management complexity.
4.Over-Indexing Risk: Too many indices can degrade performance instead of
improving it.
5.Not Always Suitable: For small tables or rarely queried columns, indices may
offer minimal benefit.

access and greatly improves lookup speed.

Optimization
 A relational algebra expression may have many equivalent expressions
 E.g., consider the query:
 select salary
 from instructor
 where salary < 75000;
 Equivalent relational-algebra expressions:
 salary<75000(salary(instructor))
 salary(salary<75000(instructor))
 Each relational algebra operation can be evaluated using one of several 
different algorithms
 Correspondingly, a relational-algebra expression can be evaluated in many 
ways.

Basic Steps in Query Processing
Optimization
 To evaluate a query, we also need not to annotate it with instructions 
specifying how to evaluate each operation. 
 Annotations may state the algorithm to be used for a specific operation or 
the particular index or indices to use. 
 A relational-algebra operation annotated with instructions on how to 
evaluate it is called an evaluation primitive. 
 A sequence of primitive operations that can be used to evaluate a query is 
a query-execution plan or query-evaluation plan.
 E.g.,:
 Use an index on salary to find instructors with salary < 75000,
 Or perform complete relation scan and discard instructors with salary 
75000.

Measures of Query Cost
 Many factors contribute to time cost
 disk access, CPU, and network communication
 Cost can be measured based on 
 response time, i.e. total elapsed time for answering query, or
 total resource consumption
 We use total resource consumption as cost metric
 Response time harder to estimate, and minimizing resource consumption is a 
good idea in a shared database
 We ignore CPU costs for simplicity
 Real systems do take CPU cost into account
 Network costs must be considered for parallel systems
 We describe how estimate the cost of each operation
 We do not include cost to writing output to disk

 But more optimistic estimates are used in practice.

Bitmap Index Scan
The bitmap index scan algorithm of PostgreSQL
 Bridges gap between secondary index scan and linear file scan when 
number of matching records is not known before execution
 Bitmap with 1 bit per page in relation
 Steps:
1. Index scan used to find record ids, and set bit of corresponding page in 
bitmap
2. Linear file scan fetching only pages with bit set to 1
 Performance
 Similar to index scan when only a few bits are set
 Similar to linear file scan when most bits are set
 Never behaves very badly compared to best alternative

slides.text:
Pipelining
 In demand driven or lazy evaluation
 system repeatedly requests next tuple from top level operation
 Each operation requests next tuple from children operations as required, in order to output its 
next tuple
 In between calls, operation has to maintain “state” so it knows what to return next
 In producer-driven or eager pipelining
 Operators produce tuples eagerly and pass them up to their parents
 Buffer maintained between operators, child puts tuples in buffer, parent removes tuples from 
buffer
 if buffer is full, child waits till there is space in the buffer, and then generates more tuples
 System schedules operations that have space in output buffer and can process more input 
tuples
 Alternative name: pull and push models of pipelining

Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
● DBMS alone cannot be responsible for maintaining the confidentiality, 
integrity, and availability of the data.
● Rather, the database works as part of a network of services, including 
applications, Web servers, firewalls, SSL terminators, and security 
monitoring systems.
● So, a database may be compromised even if it would have been perfectly 
secure on its own merits.
● Four control measures to protect databases against the threats: access 
control, inference control, flow control, and encryption.

Sensitive Data and Types of Disclosures
Sensitivity of data is a measure of the importance assigned to the data by its owner for the 
purpose of denoting its need for protection.
Several factors can cause data to be classified as sensitive:
1. Inherently sensitive: The value of the data itself may be so revealing or confidential 
that it becomes sensitive—for example, a person’s salary or whether a patient has 
HIV/AIDS.
2. From a sensitive source: The source of the data may indicate a need for secrecy—for 
example, an informer whose identity must be kept secret.
3. Declared sensitive: The owner of the data may have explicitly declared it as sensitive.
4. A sensitive attribute or sensitive record: The particular attribute or record may have

by itself but will become sensitive in the presence of some other data—for example, 
the exact latitude and longitude information for a location where some previously 
recorded event happened that was later deemed sensitive.

Sensitive Data and Types of Disclosures
Several factors must be considered before deciding whether it is safe to reveal 
the data. 
The three most important factors are data availability, access acceptability, 
and authenticity assurance.
1. Data availability: If a user is updating a field, then this field becomes 
inaccessible and other users should not be able to view this data 
(temporarily-concurrency control).
2. Access acceptability: Data should only be revealed to authorized users.
3. Authenticity assurance: Before granting access, certain external 
characteristics about the user may also be considered. For example, a 
user may only be permitted access during working hours.

the privilege on R to a third account C, also with GRANT OPTION. 
● In this way, privileges on R can propagate to other accounts without the 
knowledge of the owner of R.

Flow Control: Covert Channels
● Covert channels can be classified into two broad categories:
● Storage channels do not require any temporal synchronization, in that 
information is conveyed by accessing system information or what is 
otherwise inaccessible to the user. A storage channel example uses 
shared storage, such as a temporary directory, to allow two subjects to 
signal each other.
● Timing channel allow the information to be conveyed by the timing of 
events or processes. A covert timing channel relies on the system clock to 
infer sensitive information.
● Some security experts believe that one way to avoid covert channels is for 
programmers to not actually gain access to sensitive data that a program 
is supposed to process after the program has been put into operation.

Distributed Database Concepts
What Constitutes a DDB?
For a database to be called distributed, the following minimum conditions 
should be satisfied:
● Connection of database nodes over a computer network: There are 
multiple computers, called sites or nodes. These sites must be connected 
by an underlying network to transmit data and commands among sites.
● Logical interrelation of the connected databases: It is essential that 
the information in the various database nodes be logically related.
● Possible absence of homogeneity among connected nodes: It is not 
necessary that all nodes be identical in terms of data, hardware, and 
software.

Autonomy
● Autonomy determines the extent to which individual nodes or DBs in a

● A high degree of autonomy is desirable for increased flexibility and 
customized maintenance of an individual node. 
● Autonomy can be applied to design, communication, and execution. 
● Design autonomy refers to independence of data model usage and 
transaction management techniques among nodes. 
● Communication autonomy determines the extent to which each node 
can decide on sharing of information with other nodes. 
● Execution autonomy refers to independence of users to act as they 
please.

Distributed Database Concepts
Advantages of Distributed Databases
1. Improved ease and flexibility of application development.
2. Increased availability.
○ A distributed database system has multiple nodes (computers) and if one fails then 
others are available to do the job.
3. Improved performance.
○ A distributed DBMS fragments the database to keep data closer to where it is needed 
most (Data localization). 
○ This reduces data management (access and modification) time significantly.
4. Easier expansion via scalability. 
○ Allows new nodes (computers) to be added anytime without chaining the entire 
configuration.

Commit Protocols-Two-Phase Commit Protocol
● The Two-Phase Commit Protocol (2PC) is a widely used approach to ensure atomic 
transactions in distributed systems.
● It is a distributed transaction protocol used for ensuring data consistency and 
integrity across multiple nodes in a distributed system. 
● In 2PC, a coordinator oversees multiple participants and ensures that either all 
participants agree to commit the transaction, or if any participant fails to commit, 
all participants rollback.
● Thus, it provides atomicity and durability properties.

Commit Protocols- Two-Phase Commit Protocol Working

Transaction Management in Distributed Databases
Commit Protocols-Two-Phase Commit Protocol Working
● 2PC operates in two phases: the Prepare Phase and the Commit Phase.
● 1. Prepare Phase:
○ The coordinator sends a Prepare request to all participants.
○ Each participant checks if it can complete the transaction and responds with 
either a Yes (prepared) or No (abort).
● 2. Commit Phase:
○ If all participants respond with Yes, the coordinator sends a Commit 
command, and all participants commit the transaction.
○ If any participant responds with No, the coordinator sends an Abort command 
to rollback the transaction across all participants.

● 3PC operates in three phases: Prepare Phase, Pre-Commit Phase, and

● 2. Pre-Commit Phase(Prepare to commit/ Dissemination phase):
○ If all participants respond Yes, the coordinator sends a Pre-Commit message, 
indicating the transaction is likely to be committed.
○ Participants acknowledge the Pre-Commit, preparing to commit the 
transaction but not yet completing it.

Operating System Support for Transaction Management
The following are the main benefits of operating system (OS)-supported 
transaction management:
1. Typically, DBMSs use their own semaphores to guarantee mutually 
exclusive access to shared resources. OS-level knowledge of semaphores 
can help eliminate performance degradation.
2. Specialized hardware support for locking can be exploited to reduce 
associated costs.
3. Providing a set of common transaction support operations though the 
kernel allows application developers to focus on adding new features to 
their products as opposed to reimplementing the common functionality 
for each application.

Distributed Query Processing
1. Query Mapping
● The input query on distributed data is specified formally using a query 
language.
● It is first normalized, analyzed for semantic errors,
● simplified, and finally restructured into an algebraic query on global relations.
● This translation is largely identical to the one performed in a centralized DBMS.
2. Localization
● This stage maps the distributed query on the global schema to separate queries 
on individual fragments using data distribution and replication information.

Data Transfer Costs of Distributed Query Processing
● One issue in processing and optimizing a query in a distributed system is 
the cost of transferring data over the network.
● This data includes intermediate files that are transferred to other sites for 
further processing, as well as the final result files that may have to be 
transferred to the site where the query result is needed.
● DDBMS query optimization algorithms consider the goal of reducing the 
amount of data transfer as an optimization criterion in choosing a 
distributed query execution strategy.

Semijoin operator
● A semi join is a relational algebra operation that returns rows from the 
left table only if a matching record exists in the right table, without adding 
any columns from the right table.
● Left semi-join is denoted by (R ⋉ S).
● Key Characteristics
○ Columns Returned: Only includes columns from the left (first) table.
○ Existence Check: Acts as a filter based on whether data exists in the related 
table, ensuring each left-table row is returned at most once (unlike regular 
joins which can duplicate rows if there are multiple matches).
● Highly effective for query optimization in distributed databases, as it 
minimizes network data transfer by sending only matching keys or 
projected column lists between database sites instead of full tables.

slides.text:
Distributed Query Processing Using Semijoin
● The semijoin operation reduces the number of tuples in a relation before 
transferring it to another site.
● Intuitively, the idea is to send the joining column of one relation R to the 
site where the other relation S is located; 
● this column is then joined with S. 
● Following that, the join attributes, along with the attributes required in 
the result, are projected out and shipped back to the original site and 
joined with R.
● Hence, only the joining column of R is transferred in one direction, and a 
subset of S with no extraneous tuples or attributes is transferred in the 
other direction. If only a small fraction of the tuples in S participate in the 
join, this can be an efficient solution to minimizing data transfer.

Query and Update Decomposition
● A DDBMS that supports full distribution, fragmentation, and replication 
transparency allows the user to specify a query or update request just as 
though the DBMS were centralized. 
● For updates, the DDBMS is responsible for maintaining consistency 
among replicated items by using one of the distributed concurrency 
control algorithms. 
● For queries, a query decomposition module must break up or decompose 
a query into subqueries that can be executed at the individual sites.
● Additionally, a strategy for combining the results of the subqueries to 
form the query result must be generated.

● Whenever the DDBMS determines that an item referenced in the query is 
replicated, it must choose or materialize a particular replica during query 
execution.
● To determine which replicas include the data items referenced in a query, the
● DDBMS refers to the fragmentation, replication, and distribution information
● stored in the DDBMS catalog. 
● For vertical fragmentation, the attribute list for each fragment is kept in the 
catalog. 
● For horizontal fragmentation, a condition, sometimes called a guard, is kept 
for each fragment. 
○ This is basically a selection condition that specifies which tuples exist in the 
fragment; it is called a guard because only tuples that satisfy this condition are 
permitted to be stored in the fragment.
● For mixed fragments, both the attribute list and the guard condition are kept 
in the catalog.

● Spatial analysis operations, which often use statistical techniques, are used to

● Flow analysis operations help in determining the shortest path between two points

● Spatial search allows a user to search for objects within a particular spatial region.

Spatial Data Types
● Map data includes various geographic or spatial features of objects in a map, such as 
an object’s shape and the location of the object within the map.
● The three basic types of features are points, lines, and polygons (or areas).
● Points are used to represent spatial characteristics of objects whose locations 
correspond to a single 2-D coordinate (x, y, or longitude/latitude) in the scale of a 
particular application. 
● Some examples of point objects could be buildings, cellular towers, or stationary 
vehicles.
● Moving vehicles and other moving objects can be represented by a sequence of point 
locations that change over time. 
● Lines represent objects having length, such as roads or rivers, whose spatial 
characteristics can be approximated by a sequence of connected lines.

﻿ Different kinds of spatial analyses Spatial analysis operations, which often use statistical techniques, are used to uncover spatial relationships within and among mapped data layers.
Flow analysis operations help in determining the shortest path between two points and also the connectivity among nodes or regions in a graph.
Location analysis aims to find if the given set of points and lines lie within a given polygon (location).
Digital terrain analysis is used to build three-dimensional models, where the topography of a geographical location can be represented with an x, y, z data model known as Digital Terrain (or Elevation) Model (DTM/DEM).

﻿ Spatial Data Types Map data includes various geographic or spatial features of objects in a map, such as an object’s shape and the location of the object within the map.

Points are used to represent spatial characteristics of objects whose locations correspond to a single 2-D coordinate (x, y, or longitude/latitude) in the scale of a particular application.
Some examples of point objects could be buildings, cellular towers, or stationary vehicles.

Lines represent objects having length, such as roads or rivers, whose spatial characteristics can be approximated by a sequence of connected lines.

Example: If a polygon represents a county or district on a map, its attribute data includes text and numbers like population, largest city, and area in square miles.

﻿ Spatial Data Types Spatial Data Types — Image Data (Raster)
What it is: Overhead visual captures like satellite images and aerial photographs taken by cameras. 

How it is used: Real-world features (such as roads and buildings) are detected and drawn on top of these images. These photographic grids are classic examples of raster data.

﻿ Spatial Data Types Spatial Data Types — Vector vs. Raster
To represent the physical world inside a database, spatial data is divided into two fundamentally different formats: 

Vector Data (Drawing with Math): Represents distinct objects using exact geometric shapes—Points (a coffee shop), Lines (a highway), and Polygons (a city boundary). Because it uses mathematical coordinates, zooming in keeps the lines sharp. 

Raster Data (Coloring a Grid): Represents continuous surfaces using a matrix of tiny square cells (pixels). Satellite photos and aerial images are classic examples—zooming in far enough reveals the individual square pixels.
﻿ Models of spatial information Depending on what real-world thing you are tracking, you pick one of two data modeling approaches:

﻿ Spatial Operators Spatial Operators (How We Manipulate Shapes)
Standard SQL uses simple math operators (=, <, >). Spatial databases need geometric operators divided into four categories: 

Overview: Spatial operators capture geometric properties of objects in physical space and the relationships between them. They fall into three static categories (Topological, Projective, Metric) plus Dynamic operators. 
Operators are classified into three broad categories:
Topological operators
Projective operators
Metric operators

﻿ Spatial Operators Topological Operators (Relationships That Survive Stretching):
The Rule: Properties that stay true even if you rotate, move, or stretch the map like a rubber sheet. 

Examples: open (region), close (region), inside (point, loop). If a pin is inside a circle on a balloon, stretching the balloon doesn't change the fact that the pin is still inside.

﻿ Spatial Operators Projective operators
Shape Geometry & Angles:
The Rule: Evaluates concavity (caves/indents) and convexity (bulges) of shapes. 

Example: Convex Hull—imagine stretching a rubber band around a cluster of pins on a corkboard. The rubber band forms the tightest outer boundary around them.

﻿ Spatial Operators Metric operators
Exact Measurements:
The Rule: Measures concrete, global physical dimensions of single objects or pairs. 

Examples: length (arc), distance (point, point), area, compactness, and symmetry.

﻿ Spatial Operators Dynamic Spatial Operators
Editing & Moving Objects:
The Rule: Operations that actually alter, move, or destroy spatial objects. 

Basic CRUD: create, destroy, update. 

Geometric Updates: translate (shift position), rotate (spin), scale (resize up/down), reflect (mirror image), and shear (slant/deform).

﻿ Spatial Ǫueries Overview: Spatial queries are requests for spatial data that rely on spatial operations, grouped into three types.

Three types:
Range queries
Nearest neighbor queries
Spatial joins or overlays

﻿ Spatial Ǫueries Range queries
Search Inside a Bubble): Finds all objects of a specific type inside a given boundary or radius. 

Example: "Find all ambulances within a five-mile radius of an accident location."

﻿ Spatial Ǫueries Nearest neighbor queries
Find the Closest One): Finds the single object of a specific type closest to a given location. 

Example: "Find the police car that is closest to the location of a crime."

﻿ Spatial Ǫueries Spatial joins or overlays
Matching Two Map Layers): Joins two different object types based on a spatial condition like intersecting, overlapping, or distance. 

Example: Joining railway station objects and hotel objects to find all hotels within 5 kilometers of a railway station.

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing A spatial database system needs an index mechanism that will help it retrieve data items quickly according to their spatial locations.
Traditional indexing methods are not well suited to data objects of non-zero size located in multidimensional spaces.

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing A spatial index is used to organize objects into a set of buckets.
The buckets correspond to pages of secondary memory), so that objects in a particular spatial region can be easily located.
Each bucket has a bucket region, a part of space containing all objects stored in the bucket.
The bucket regions are usually rectangles.
For point data structures, these regions are disjoint and they partition the space so that each point belongs to precisely one bucket.
There are essentially two:

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Specialized indexing structures that allow efficient search for data objects based on spatial search operations are included in the database system.
Similar to B+-tree indexes in traditional database systems.
Examples of these indexing structures are grid files and R-trees.
Spatial join indexes, can be used to speed up spatial join operations.
The two-dimensional (2-D) spatial data is converted to single-dimensional (1-D) data.
so that traditional indexing techniques (B+-tree) can be used.
The algorithms for converting from 2-D to 1-D are known as space filling curves.
﻿ Spatial Data Indexing

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Grid Files
A grid file is a multi-dimensional data structure used to handle indexing
and efficient querying across two or more search keys simultaneously.
It acts as a symmetric multi-key indexing scheme.
Records are visualized as points in an n-dimensional space.
where each dimension represents the domain of a specific attribute.
e.g., latitude, longitude, or age and salary.
The search space is split into a grid using linear scales along each axis.
The actual data records are grouped and stored in data buckets on the disk.
Multiple grid cells (regions of the multi-dimensional space) can point to the same bucket if they share space or if data density is low.

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Grid Files
They can also be used for indexing n-dimensional spatial data.
The fixed-grid method divides an n-dimensional hyperspace into equal size buckets.
The data structure that implements the fixed grid is an n-dimensional array.
The objects whose spatial locations lie within a cell (totally or partially) can be stored in a dynamic structure to handle overflows.
Useful for uniformly distributed data like satellite imagery.
The fixed-grid structure is rigid, and its directory can be sparse and large.

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing R-trees
A height-balanced tree.
An extension of the B+-tree for k-dimensions, where k > 1.
Designed for spatial data storage and multi-dimensional indexing.
spatial objects are approximated in the R-tree by their minimum bounding rectangle (MBR).
MBR is the smallest rectangle, with sides parallel to the coordinate system (x and y) axis, that contains the object.

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing R-trees: Properties
Consists of a single root, internals nodes, and leaf nodes.
The root contains the pointer to the largest region in the spatial domain.
Parent nodes contains pointers to their child nodes where the region of child nodes completely overlaps the regions of parent nodes.
Leaf nodes contains data about the MBR to the current objects.
MBR-Minimum bounding region refers to the minimal bounding box parameter surrounding the region/object under consideration.
﻿ Spatial Data Indexing R-trees: Example

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Quad-trees
A tree data structure.
used to partition a two-dimensional space into smaller regions.
each node in the tree has four children, corresponding to the four quadrants of the space.
useful for spatial indexing and searching.
It allows efficient insertion, deletion, and retrieval of objects based on their spatial location.
It can efficiently handle spatial queries such as range searches and nearest neighbor searches.
Applications: GIS, computer graphics, video games, image processing.

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Quad-trees
The quadtree starts with a root node that represents the entire space.
Each level of the tree divides the space into four equal-sized quadrants.
Each node of a Quad Tree has at most four children.
The leaf nodes of the tree represent smaller regions of the space.

﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Quad-trees: Construction
Divide the current two-dimensional space into four boxes.
If a box contains one or more points in it, create a child object, storing in it the two-dimensional space of the box.
If a box does not contain any points, do not create a child for it.
Recurse for each of the children.
﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Quad-trees
﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Quad-trees
﻿ Spatial Data Indexing Comparison: B-tree vs. R-tree vs. Quad-tree
﻿ Spatial Data Mining

﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial Classification
Definition: Estimate attribute values based on other attributes
Also called location prediction problem
Examples:
Predicting nest locations in wetlands (vegetation durability, water depth)
Identifying crime hotspots
﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial Classification

﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial Association
Definition: Rules based on spatial predicates
Rule format:
Example: is_a(x, country) ∧ touches(x, Mediterranean) ⇒ is_a(x, wine-exporter)
Key differences from non-spatial associations:
No clear "transactions" (continuous space)
Smaller item sets
Spatial items often discretized (e.g., income regions)
﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial Association

﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial Colocation Rules
Generalize association rules to spatially indexed datasets
Useful for analyzing point collections (e.g., income regions, disease spread)

﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial Clustering
Definition: Group objects so similar ones cluster together
Application: Group seismic events → identify earthquake faults
Algorithms:
DBSCAN: Finds clusters based on density distribution
DENCLUE: Uses density functions to detect clusters
﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial Clustering: DBSCAN

﻿ Spatial Data Mining Spatial data mining reveals hidden patterns in correlated spatial data
Techniques:
Classification → Predict locations
Association → Discover spatial rules
Clustering → Identify dense regions
Applications: Ecology, crime analysis, geology, urban planning
﻿ Applications of Spatial Data

﻿ Introduction Growth of mobile computing and smartphones
Need for data availability on the move
Examples: WhatsApp, Uber, Mobile Banking, E-commerce apps
Challenges: limited resources, connectivity issues, security

﻿ Mobile Computing Environment Definition: “A computing environment where users access data, 	applications, and services through mobile devices over wireless 	networks.”
Components:
Mobile devices (smartphones, tablets, wearables)
Wireless networks (Wi-Fi, 4G/5G, Bluetooth)
Cloud services & backend servers
Characteristics:
Ubiquity (anytime, anywhere access)
Resource constraints (battery, storage, bandwidth)
Dynamic connectivity (handoffs, roaming)

﻿ Mobile Computing Architecture A distributed architecture where a number of computers, generally referred to as Fixed Hosts and Base Stations, are interconnected through a high-speed wired network.
Fixed hosts are general purpose computers that are not typically equipped to manage mobile units but can be configured to do so.
Base stations function as gateways to the fixed network for the Mobile Units.
They are equipped with wireless interfaces and offer network access services of which mobile units are clients.
﻿ Mobile Computing Architecture

﻿ Mobile Computing Architecture Layers of Architecture:
Mobile Device Layer – hardware, OS, local DB (e.g., SQLite)
Network Layer – wireless communication, protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP, MQTT)
Middleware Layer – synchronization, caching, security services
Server/Cloud Layer – enterprise DBMS, application servers, APIs

Example: WhatsApp message flow (device → internet → server → recipient)
﻿ Mobile Computing Architecture

﻿ Mobile Databases Mobile Database is a database that is transportable, portable, and physically separate or detached from the corporate database server but has the capability to communicate with those servers from remote sites allowing the sharing of various kinds of data.
Mobile databases are databases designed to operate on mobile devices or in mobile environments, enabling data access, synchronization, and management anytime, anywhere.
With mobile databases, users have access to corporate data on their laptop, PDA, or other Internet access device that is required for applications at remote sites.

﻿ Mobile Databases Mobile Database typically involves three parties:
Fixed Hosts -
It performs the transactions and data management functions with the help of database servers.
Mobiles Units -
These are portable computers that move around a geographical region that includes the cellular network that these units use to communicate to base stations.
Base Stations -
These are two-way radios installation in fixed locations, that pass communication with the mobile units to and from the fixed hosts.

﻿ Characteristics of Mobile Environments Portability
Lower bandwidth
Range, interference
Locality of access
Support for packet switching
High communication latency
Limited storage & processing power
Frequent disconnections
Synchronization with central servers
Security & privacy concerns

﻿ Data Management Issues Connectivity Issues
Frequent disconnections, variable bandwidth
Consistency & Synchronization
Conflict resolution in replicated data
Resource Constraints
Limited CPU, memory, battery
Security & Privacy
Protecting sensitive data on mobile devices
Scalability
Handling millions of concurrent mobile users
Data Distribution
Managing data across heterogeneous devices and networks

﻿ Data Synchronization Why synchronization is needed?
Techniques:
Two-way sync
Conflict detection & resolution
Replication strategies
Example: Google Drive oﬄine sync
﻿ Data Synchronization

﻿ Ǫuery Processing in Mobile Databases Constraints: low bandwidth, limited CPU
Query optimization for mobile
Use of caching and indexing
Example: location-based queries in ride-hailing apps

﻿ Security in Mobile Databases Threats: unauthorized access, data leakage
Techniques:
Authentication & authorization
Encryption (at rest & in transit)
Secure APIs
Example: Mobile banking apps

﻿ Types of Mobile Databases Local Databases (SQLite, Realm)
Remote Databases (Firebase, AWS DynamoDB)
Hybrid Approaches (oﬄine-first with sync)
Examples in real-world apps

﻿ Popular Mobile Database Systems SQLite – lightweight, embedded
Realm – object-oriented, oﬄine-first
Firebase Realtime Database – cloud-hosted, sync across clients
Couchbase Mobile – NoSQL, sync with Couchbase Server

﻿ Applications of Mobile Databases Social media apps
Mobile commerce
Healthcare apps (patient records)
IoT & sensor data collection
Travel & navigation apps

ADMT EXAM PREPARATION GUIDE • MODULE 4
Distributed Databases: Part 1 Study Guide
Complete plain-English translation, human-level analogies, relational algebra, and architectural
breakdowns.
1. Foundational Concepts & Definition
A Distributed Database (DDB) is a collection of multiple, logically related database files physically spread
across different computers (called sites or nodes) interconnected by a computer network.
The managing software is the Distributed Database Management System (DDBMS). Its primary objective
is to coordinate the distributed processing of transactions while making the underlying network
completely transparent to users and application developers.
MINIMUM CONDITIONS FOR A TRUE DDB (EXAM CHECKLIST)
A system is only classified as a distributed database if it satisfies three strict criteria:
Network Interconnection: Nodes must be connected via LAN or WAN to transmit data,
commands, and synchronization messages.
Logical Interrelation: The data stored on different machines must belong to the same logical
business enterprise (e.g., regional bank branches belonging to one banking system).
No Requirement for Homogeneity: Sites do not need identical hardware, operating systems, or
DBMS software engines.
2. Demystifying "Transparency"
In standard conversational English, "transparent" means glass-like visibility. In database engineering,
transparency means invisibility: the technical mechanics of the network and physical storage are hidden
so the entire distributed system behaves like a single, local database on one laptop.
Transparency Type Plain-English Meaning & Practical Application
Distribution / Network Users write queries without knowing network protocols, cable paths, or hardware
topologies.
Location Transparency Commands execute identically regardless of where the user is physically located
or where the data physically resides.
Naming Transparency Objects (e.g., EMPLOYEES) have a single logical name. You do not need to query
Server_Mumbai.DB.EMPLOYEES.
Replication Transparency Users and queries are unaware that duplicate copies exist. The system
automatically reads from the nearest copy and updates all replicas.
Fragmentation
Transparency
Queries are written against full tables. Users do not need to know that rows or
columns are partitioned into separate fragments.
Design & Execution Hides the physical layout design and prevents users from needing to coordinate
where sub-queries physically run.
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 1 Study Guide Page 1 of 6

3. System Stability: Fault, Error, and Failure
Textbooks often explain these terms in reverse order. Understanding them requires walking forward along
the causal chain:
THE AUTOMOTIVE DOMINO CHAIN
1. Fault (The Root Cause): A sharp nail punctures a vehicle's tire. (In software: a code bug, bad disk
sector, or loose Ethernet cable).
2. Error (The Bad Internal State): The tire pressure drops to 5 PSI. The car is still driving, but its internal
state is now invalid. (In a DB: corrupted data in RAM or a dropped packet).
3. Failure (The Visible Crash): The tire blows out completely and the vehicle halts on the highway. (In a
DB: the server crashes, aborts, or outputs incorrect query results).
Reliability vs. Availability:
Reliability: A point-in-time measurement. The probability that the system is fully operating and
delivering correct service at a specific instant (e.g., "Will it process a payment at 3:00:00 PM without
crashing?").
Availability: A time-interval measurement. The probability that the system is continuously operational
across an entire span of time (e.g., 99.99% uptime over a 30-day billing cycle).
4. Scalability, Partition Tolerance & Node Autonomy
Scalability: The ability to expand system processing capacity without service downtime.
Horizontal Scalability (Scale Out): Adding more physical machines/nodes to the network cluster.
Vertical Scalability (Scale Up): Adding more RAM, faster CPUs, or bigger SSDs to an existing single
machine.
Partition Tolerance: The ability of a distributed database to continue functioning even when network
communication between sites is severed, splitting the network into isolated sub-networks.
The 4 Autonomy Dimensions (Node Independence)
Autonomy defines the degree of freedom an individual site retains while participating in a distributed
system:
Design Autonomy: Freedom of a site to choose its own data model (relational vs document), schema
definitions, and transaction rules.
Communication Autonomy: Freedom of a site to decide whether, when, and how it communicates or
shares data with other nodes.
Execution Autonomy: Freedom of a site to prioritize and execute its own local user operations without
interference or throttling from external global requests.
Association Autonomy: Freedom of a site to decide how much of its internal functionality and private
data it exposes to the global network.
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 1 Study Guide Page 2 of 6

5. Data Fragmentation: Rules & Relational Algebra
Fragmentation is the process of breaking a global relation R into smaller logical units called fragments.
This improves data localization (placing records close to frequent users), boosts parallel execution, and
enforces security by not storing sensitive fields on remote branch servers.
THE 3 CORRECTNESS RULES OF FRAGMENTATION (EXAM FAVORITE)
Whenever a relation R is split into fragments {F1
, F2
, ..., Fn
}, it must satisfy:
1. Completeness: Every single data item (tuple or attribute) present in R must be present in at least
one fragment. No data is lost.
2. Reconstruction: There must exist a relational algebra expression (using ∪ or ⋈) that reconstructs
the original relation R perfectly from its fragments.
3. Disjointness: Data should not overlap unnecessarily. In horizontal fragmentation, no tuple can
appear in more than one fragment. In vertical fragmentation, fragments must share only the
primary key.
The 3 Types of Fragmentation

6. Schemas & Replication Strategies
A distributed database separates design structure into two dedicated blueprints:
Fragmentation Schema: Defines how tables are logically partitioned (the selection conditions and
column projection lists) and records the algebraic reconstruction rules. It knows nothing about
physical IP addresses or server hardware.
Allocation Schema: The mapping catalog that specifies where each fragment (and its copies) is
physically stored across network sites.
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 1 Study Guide Page 3 of 6

Data Replication Approaches
Fully Replicated: Every site stores a complete copy of the entire database. Highest read availability and
speed, but worst update performance because every modification must be synchronized everywhere
over the network.
Non-Redundant (Partitioned / Zero Replication): Each fragment lives on exactly one site. Storage￾efficient and fast for local updates, but zero fault tolerance—if that node crashes, its data is completely
offline.
Partial Replication: High-traffic fragments are replicated across multiple sites, while rarely accessed
records remain on a single site. The industry standard balance.
7. DDBMS Classification & Semantic Heterogeneity
Distributed database systems are categorized by software homogeneity and autonomy:
1. Homogeneous DDBMS
Every node runs the exact same DBMS software engine (e.g., all Oracle or all PostgreSQL). The operating
systems can differ (one node runs Linux, another Windows, another Unix), but identical DBMS software
makes query compilation, catalog lookups, and transaction coordination straightforward.
2. Heterogeneous DDBMS (Federated vs. Multidatabase)
Nodes run different database software and potentially different underlying data models (mixing relational,
object-oriented, and legacy hierarchical engines). Usually arises when independent companies merge or
distinct departments integrate legacy databases.
Federated Database: Sites retain significant local autonomy (deciding what data to share and
executing local tasks first), but all sites access data through a single, centralized conceptual schema.
Gateways translate between local engines and the global interface.
Multidatabase (Peer-to-Peer): There is no single global conceptual schema. Applications construct
ad-hoc schemas dynamically on the fly as needed.
SEMANTIC HETEROGENEITY (DIFFERENCES IN MEANING)
The primary challenge in federated systems is reconciling conflicting semantic interpretations:
Naming Clashes: Synonyms (Site 1 calls an attribute Cust_ID, Site 2 calls it ClientID) and
homonyms (Rate means hourly pay rate at Site 1, but interest rate at Site 2).
Unit & Currency Discrepancies: Site 1 stores salary in USD; Site 2 stores salary in INR.
Business Rule Differences: Site 1 classifies an employee as "Active" if currently assigned to a
project; Site 2 classifies them as "Active" if paid within the last 60 days.
8. Hardware & Software Architectures
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 1 Study Guide Page 4 of 6

Multiprocessor Hardware Models
Shared-Memory (Tightly Coupled): All CPUs share common RAM and disk storage via a high-speed
system bus. High memory contention risk.
Shared-Disk (Loosely Coupled): Each CPU has private RAM, but all nodes share a common disk
storage array over a network.
Shared-Nothing (Distributed Baseline): Every node has its own independent CPU, private RAM, and
local disk. Nodes communicate solely via message passing over the network. Most scalable
architecture.
Software Managers in Pure DDBMS
Global Query Compiler: Consults the Global System Catalog to parse queries, verify schema
semantics, and enforce global integrity constraints.
Global Query Optimizer: Evaluates candidate execution plans to generate optimized sub-queries for
local sites, specifically minimizing network communication cost.
Global Transaction Manager: Coordinates execution across local transaction managers to ensure
multi-site transactions commit or abort atomically.
The 4-Layer Schema Hierarchy
1. External Views: Customized logical views exposed to client applications.
2. Global Conceptual Schema (GCS): Unified definition of all data enterprise-wide as if it were a single
centralized database.
3. Local Conceptual Schema (LCS): Logical schema of the specific fragment stored at that individual
node.
4. Local Internal Schema (LIS): Physical disk organization, access paths, and indexes on that specific
local machine.
9. The 7 Classic Design Issues in DDBMS
1. Distributed Database Design: Deciding optimal fragmentation and allocation of data across sites to
minimize storage, processing, and communication costs.
2. Distributed Directory (Catalog) Management: Deciding whether the system "address book" is
centralized (single point of failure) or distributed/replicated (high update overhead).
3. Distributed Query Processing: Decomposing queries and pushing data selection/filtering down to local
sites before transmission over slow network links to avoid network bottlenecks.
4. Distributed Concurrency Control: Synchronizing simultaneous data access across replicas using
fundamental primitives:
Locking (Pessimistic): Blocks concurrent access to prevent conflicts. Requires designated
coordinator sites or majority voting.
Timestamps (Optimistic): Orders transactions chronologically using start timestamps; aborts out￾of-order execution.
5. Distributed Deadlock Management: Detecting and resolving cycles of waiting transactions spread
across multiple network sites using detection, prevention, avoidance, or victim selection recovery.
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 1 Study Guide Page 5 of 6

6. Reliability: Preserving ACID consistency across site crashes and communication link failures using
distributed recovery and commit protocols.
7. Replication Protocols: Synchronizing data copies across nodes using either Eager (Synchronous)
replication (ensures instant consistency before commit) or Lazy (Asynchronous) replication (fast
background updates).
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 1 Study Guide Page 6 of 6

ADMT EXAM PREPARATION GUIDE • MODULE 4 (PART 2)
Distributed Databases: Concurrency, Transactions
& Query Optimization
Plain-English guide covering distributed locking, commit handshakes (2PC/3PC), OS primitives, query
stages, and decomposition.
1. Distributed Concurrency Control: The Challenges
In a centralized database, concurrency control is simple: manage locks in local RAM. In a distributed
database, five distinct network complications arise:
Multiple Replicas: Data copies living at different sites must reflect identical values. An update cannot
leave copies in an inconsistent state.
Individual Site Failures: If a node goes offline, the remaining sites must continue servicing
transactions. When the failed node reboots, it must synchronize its local data before rejoining.
Communication Link Failures & Partitioning: Network cables or routers can fail, splitting nodes into
isolated sub-networks that cannot communicate.
Distributed Commit: A transaction that touched data across three sites must never commit on two
sites while rolling back on the third.
Distributed Deadlocks: Transactions on different sites can be waiting on each other in a circular chain
across the network.
2. Distributed Locking Strategies
Concurrency control relies on two fundamental paradigms for managing locks across replicated data:
A. Concurrency Control Based on a Distinguished Copy (Master Approaches)
Instead of requesting permission from every site holding a copy, a specific copy is chosen as the
"distinguished copy" to coordinate all locks:
Primary Site Technique: One single, designated server across the entire enterprise holds the lock
manager for all data items. Limitation: Massive bottleneck and a single point of failure.
Primary Site with Backup: An active primary site manages all locks, while a shadow/backup site
mirrors lock states continuously. If the primary site dies, the backup immediately takes over.
Primary Copy Method: The master role is distributed by data item. Server 1 coordinates locks for Table
A, Server 2 coordinates locks for Table B, and Server 3 coordinates locks for Table C. This distributes
lock traffic evenly.
Coordinator Election: In any distinguished copy setup, if the coordinator site goes down and no
designated backup exists, surviving sites run an Election Algorithm to vote in a replacement
coordinator.
B. Voting / Majority Locking (Democratic Approach)
There is no distinguished copy or master coordinator. When a transaction requests a lock, it sends lock
request messages to every site holding a replica of that item.
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 2 Study Guide Page 1 of 5

Each site manages its own local lock table and grants/denies the local lock.
If the transaction secures a strict majority (> 50%) of affirmative lock votes, it officially holds the lock
across the entire system.
Trade-off: High fault tolerance (no single point of failure), but significantly higher network message
traffic.
3. Transaction Management & The Global Transaction Manager (GTM)
When a transaction accesses data across multiple sites, the site where the transaction originated
temporarily assumes the role of the Global Transaction Manager (Coordinator). It coordinates with local
transaction managers to enforce ACID properties:
BEGIN_TRANSACTION: Registers a globally unique transaction ID.
READ: Directs the query to an available, valid local or nearby replica.
WRITE: Ensures updates propagate to all replicas across the network.
COMMIT / ABORT: Executes atomic termination protocols across all participating sites.
4. Atomic Commit Protocols: 2PC vs. 3PC
Two-Phase Commit Protocol (2PC)
The standard atomic commitment protocol. It operates in two sequential phases:
1. Phase 1: Prepare Phase (Voting): The coordinator broadcasts a Prepare to Commit request to all
participant nodes. Each participant executes checks locally, writes logs, and votes YES (Prepared) or
NO (Abort).
2. Phase 2: Commit / Abort Phase (Decision):
If all participants vote YES, the coordinator broadcasts GLOBAL COMMIT. Participants commit
locally and reply with an ACK.
If even one participant votes NO (or times out), the coordinator broadcasts GLOBAL ABORT. All
participants roll back.
THE CRITICAL FLAW OF 2PC: THE BLOCKING PROBLEM
Once a participant votes YES, it enters the Prepared state and cannot decide to commit or abort on its
own. If the coordinator crashes before sending the Phase 2 decision, all participants remain indefinitely
blocked, holding locks and freezing access for other users until the coordinator recovers.
Three-Phase Commit Protocol (3PC)
3PC eliminates 2PC's blocking flaw by splitting the commit phase into two sub-phases and introducing
coordinated timeouts:
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 2 Study Guide Page 2 of 5

1. Phase 1: Can-Commit Phase (Voting): Identical to 2PC. Coordinator asks participants if they can
commit; participants vote YES or NO.
2. Phase 2: Pre-Commit Phase (Dissemination): If all voted YES, the coordinator broadcasts PRE￾COMMIT. Participants acknowledge that all sites voted YES and prepare to finalize.
3. Phase 3: Do-Commit Phase (Decision): Coordinator receives acknowledgments and broadcasts
GLOBAL COMMIT.
Why 3PC is Non-Blocking: Because every participant in the Pre-Commit phase knows that unanimous
agreement was already reached, if the coordinator crashes, participants do not wait forever. Their local
timeout mechanisms fire, allowing surviving participants to elect a leader and safely finalize the commit
autonomously.
Feature Two-Phase Commit (2PC) Three-Phase Commit (3PC)
Phases 2 (Prepare, Commit/Abort) 3 (Can-Commit, Pre-Commit, Do￾Commit)
Coordinator Crash Blocks indefinitely; resources stay
locked
Non-blocking; breaks deadlocks via
timeouts
Message Overhead Low (fewer round-trip network
messages)
High (requires extra network
communication rounds)
Practical Use Financial systems, enterprise relational
databases
Highly failure-prone distributed
networks, microservices
5. Operating System Support for Transaction Management
Instead of the DBMS simulating synchronization and transaction mechanics in slow user-space software,
the underlying OS and CPU can assist:
OS-Level Semaphores: Using native OS kernel semaphores eliminates the performance hit of constant
context switching between DBMS threads and the OS scheduler.
Hardware Support for Locking: Utilizing atomic CPU instructions (such as Compare-And-Swap) allows
memory locking at the physical bus speed in a single clock cycle, removing software lock-checking
loops.
Kernel-Level Transaction APIs: Providing transaction operations (like commit and rollback routines)
directly in the OS kernel saves database developers from reimplementing basic transaction plumbing.
6. Distributed Query Processing Stages & Decomposition
When a distributed query is submitted, it is executed through four distinct pipeline stages:
1. Query Mapping (Central Site): Parses the input SQL, validates syntax/semantics against the global
schema, and generates a normalized algebraic query tree.
2. Localization (Central Site): Consults the catalog to replace global table references with their actual
constituent fragments and algebraic reconstruction rules.
3. Global Query Optimization (Central Site): Evaluates candidate execution strategies. Because network
communication cost across WAN links is the dominant expense, it generates plans that push data
filtering down to local sites before transmission.
Module 4: Distributed Databases — Part 2 Study Guide Page 3 of 5

4. Local Query Optimization (Local Sites): Each local site optimizes its local sub-query execution (index
scans, buffer allocations) using standard centralized engine techniques.
Query Decomposition & The Catalog
The query decomposition module breaks global queries into local sub-queries. It relies on metadata
stored in the system catalog:
Materializing Replicas: For read operations on replicated data, the optimizer selects the single
fastest/closest replica to read from. For updates, it routes write operations to all replicas.
Vertical Fragments: Tracked via the catalog's Attribute List to ensure queries access only sites hosting
the requested columns.
Horizontal Fragments (The Guard Condition): The catalog associates each fragment with a Guard—a
logical selection condition (e.g., Dept = 5). The optimizer evaluates the query predicate against these
guards to avoid querying sites that cannot contain matching records.
7. The Semijoin Operator (⋉)
The Semijoin (R ⋉ S) returns only the rows of R that have a matching key in S, without appending columns
from S. It acts as an existence filter.
In distributed databases, instead of transmitting an entire table over the network for a join, a semijoin
ships only the joining key column to the remote site, filters the records locally, and ships back only the
exact matching rows. Note: Semijoin is not commutative (R ⋉ S ≠ S ⋉ R).

Components of Hadoop ecosystem: HDFS
● HDFS has two core components, i.e. NameNode and DataNode. 
○ The NameNode is the main node and it doesn’t store the actual data. It contains 
metadata, just like a log file or you can say as a table of content. Therefore, it requires less 
storage and high computational resources.
○ On the other hand, all your data is stored on the DataNodes and hence it requires more 
storage resources. These DataNodes are commodity hardware (like your laptops and 
desktops) in the distributed environment. That’s the reason, why Hadoop solutions are 
very cost effective.
○ You always communicate to the NameNode while writing the data. Then, it internally 
sends a request to the client to store and replicate data on various DataNodes.

Components of Hadoop ecosystem: APACHE OOZIE
● Consider Apache Oozie as a clock and alarm service inside Hadoop Ecosystem. 
● For Apache jobs, Oozie has been just like a scheduler. 
● It schedules Hadoop jobs and binds them together as one logical work.
● There are two kinds of Oozie jobs:
● Oozie workflow: These are sequential set of actions to be executed. You can 
assume it as a relay race. Where each athlete waits for the last one to complete his 
part.
● Oozie Coordinator: These are the Oozie jobs which are triggered when the data is 
made available to it. Think of this as the response-stimuli system in our body. In the 
same manner as we respond to an external stimulus, an Oozie coordinator 
responds to the availability of data and it rests otherwise.

slides.text:
MapReduce Framework
How does MapReduce work?
A MapReduce system is usually composed of three steps (even though it's 
generalized as the combination of Map and Reduce operations/functions). The 
MapReduce operations are:
● Map: The input data is first split into smaller blocks. The Hadoop 
framework then decides how many mappers to use, based on the size of 
the data to be processed and the memory block available on each 
mapper server. Each block is then assigned to a mapper for processing. 
Each ‘worker’ node applies the map function to the local data, and writes 
the output to temporary storage. The primary (master) node ensures that 
only a single copy of the redundant input data is processed.

MapReduce Framework
How does MapReduce work?
● Shuffle, combine and partition: worker nodes redistribute data based 
on the output keys (produced by the map function), such that all data 
belonging to one key is located on the same worker node. As an optional 
process the combiner (a reducer) can run individually on each mapper 
server to reduce the data on each mapper even further making reducing 
the data footprint and shuffling and sorting easier. Partition (not optional) 
is the process that decides how the data has to be presented to the 
reducer and also assigns it to a particular reducer.

slides.text:
MapReduce Framework
How does MapReduce work?
● Reduce: A reducer cannot start while a mapper is still in progress. Worker 
nodes process each group of <key,value> pairs output data, in parallel to 
produce <key,value> pairs as output. All the map output values that have 
the same key are assigned to a single reducer, which then aggregates the 
values for that key. Unlike the map function which is mandatory to filter 
and sort the initial data, the reduce function is optional.

environments.

YARN architecture
Apache Hadoop YARN Architecture consists of the following main components :
1. Resource Manager: Runs on a master daemon and manages the resource 
allocation in the cluster.
2. Node Manager: They run on the slave daemons and are responsible for the 
execution of a task on every single Data Node.
3. Application Master: Manages the user job lifecycle and resource needs of 
individual applications. It works along with the Node Manager and monitors the 
execution of tasks.
4. Container: Package of resources including RAM, CPU, Network, HDD etc on a 
single node.

currently used as Schedulers in ResourceManager.

Role of YARN in resource management
● YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator) is the resource management and job 
scheduling layer of Apache Hadoop. 
● It manages cluster resources such as CPU and memory and allocates them to 
applications running in a Hadoop cluster.
Key roles of YARN
1. Resource Management: Tracks available CPU, memory, and other resources across 
cluster nodes.
2. Job Scheduling: Decides when and where applications should run based on resource 
availability and scheduling policies.
3. Resource Allocation: Allocates resources to applications using containers, which 
provide the resources needed to execute tasks.
4. Application Management: Manages the application execution lifecycle, from 
submission to completion.
5. Load Distribution: Distributes workloads across multiple nodes to use cluster resources 
efficiently.
6. Fault Tolerance: Helps detect failed application components and supports restarting or 
rescheduling tasks when necessary.

Graph components:
● Nodes (or vertices) represent entities (e.g., people, products, locations).
● Edges are the relationships between nodes (e.g., "friend with," "purchased

● Properties store additional information (e.g., a "friend with" relationship 
could have a "since" property to indicate when the relationship was 
established).

parent-child relationships, actions, ownership, and the like. There is no limit to 
the number and kind of relationships a node can have.
